newsitem.title: USA: FBI offers reward for Olympic bomber.
newsitem.headline: FBI offers reward for Olympic bomber.

text.p: The Federal Bureau of Investigation pleaded for help Monday in solving the Olympic bombing, offering a reward of up to $500,000 for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the bomber or bombers.

The FBI made public a recording of the telephone call made 22 minutes before the Olympic bombing and displayed a green military-style knapsack similar to the one that contained a bomb that weighed more than 40 lbs (18 kg).

"We firmly believe that somewhere, someone has a photograph of this person carrying this bomb into the park," FBI deputy director Weldon Kennedy said. "They may not know it. They may not realise they have it."

The FBI announced it would pay "up to $500,000" for photographs, videotapes or information leading to the person who planted the bomb on July 27 at Centennial Olympic Park during the 1996 Olympic Games.
Announcing the reward at a news conference in Atlanta, Kennedy called the bombing, which killed two people and injured more than 100, a "vicious crime" and appealed to the public for help.

In releasing a recording of the call made to 911 the night of the explosion, the FBI said it hoped that someone would recognise the male voice that said: "There is a bomb in Centennial Park. You have 30 minutes."
Kennedy said the backpack containing the bomb was brought into the park in the hour before the telephone call.

"The pack containing the bomb was a heavy load," he said. "Members of the public may have seen or taken a video or photo of the bomber or bombers carrying this pack on his or her back or over his or her shoulder."
"A person carrying such a pack may have been very noticeable," Kennedy said.

Casualties from the bomb might have been greater if a concert-goer had not "nudged" the backpack as it sat near a light and sound tower. "Indeed that turned out to be very fortunate, if in fact it was moved from the vertical position to the horizontal position, because no doubt that movement saved a lot of lives," Kennedy said.
The FBI denied the investigation had stalled and said its agents had interviewed hundreds of possible witnesses and reviewed thousands of photographs and videotapes.
"This investigation continues to have our highest priority," Kennedy said.

The agency asked for any photographs or videotapes taken in Olympic Park on Friday July 26 or Saturday July 27, and set up a toll-free hotline, 1-888-324-9797, for anyone with information about the bombing.

Security guard Richard Jewell, who alerted authorities to a knapsack containing the bomb, was initially identified as a suspect but was cleared on Oct. 26. Jewell's attorney, Lin Wood, said information presented by the FBI on Monday "points away from Richard Jewell."
"It shows how unfair Richard was treated," Wood said. "They had much of this information from day one of the investigation."
A threatened libel lawsuit against NBC television over remarks made about Jewell has been settled, Wood said, but both sides have agreed to keep terms of the settlement confidential.
